exp.0:0:
Paul presents himself as an apostle, that is, someone sent out with a mission and with authority. He makes clear that his calling did not come from men or through any man, but from Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, a region in Asia Minor. At the beginning he defends his authority, because some were questioning his message. Later in the letter it becomes clear that he was speaking about the gospel of grace. Here he supports that message by pointing to the resurrection of Jesus. Exactly who was challenging him is explained in several ways, but the letter shows that there was pressure to change the gospel.

Today we can ask where what we believe comes from. Rather than following trends or human opinions, let us seek what God has revealed in Jesus Christ and in his Word, and live with that confidence.
exp.0:3:
It says that Jesus Christ gave himself, that is, gave his life, because of our sins. He did this to deliver us from this present evil world, meaning this age or this world marked by evil. And all of this was according to the will of God, whom Paul calls our Father.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia together with other brothers. In the greeting, he summarizes the gospel in one sentence. Soon, in verse 6, he will show his concern that some were turning away to a different gospel. That is why he reminds them from the start that salvation comes from what Christ did, not from what we manage to accomplish.

For today: when you feel pressured by the world or by guilt, remember that Jesus has already paid for your sins. Rest in his grace and live grateful, without trying to earn God's love.
exp.0:9:
Paul asks questions to make something clear: is he trying to win the favor of people or of God? He says that if he were still trying to please men, he would not be a servant of Christ.

Pablo escribe a las iglesias de Galacia... — translated below.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were preaching a different gospel. It seems they accused him of softening the message to be liked. So he reminds them that his message does not change according to what people think and that it comes from Christ, as he explains in the verses that follow.

Today we might ask ourselves: whom do I want to please when I speak or make decisions? Being kind to everyone is good, but we must not change the truth or our faithfulness to Christ just to be accepted.
exp.0:12:
Paul reminds the Galatians of what they already knew about his past life. When he practiced Judaism, he persecuted the church of God beyond measure, meaning in an extreme way, and tried to destroy it. His way of living at that time was known to them.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were teaching a different gospel. He insists that his message did not come from people, but from Jesus Christ himself. He mentions his past to show that he could not have invented or learned this gospel from others: before, he was an enemy of the faith. Only an encounter with Christ could change him.

For today: no one is too far away for God to transform. If you have a past you are ashamed of, offer it to God with humility. And if you know someone who seems closed to faith, keep praying for that person with hope.
exp.0:16:
Paul says that, after God called him, he did not go up right away to Jerusalem to see those who were already apostles before him. Instead, he went away into Arabia and then returned again to Damascus.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some doubted his authority. He defends that he received the gospel directly from Christ, not from human leaders. Where he stayed in Arabia and what he did there is not explained in the text; some think it was a time of prayer and reflection, but that is a guess.

For today: before rushing into serving or offering opinions, it is wise to set aside time to be alone with God, to listen to his Word, and to let him confirm our faith. The counsel of others helps, but our foundation is Christ himself.
exp.0:17:
Paul says that three years after the events in Damascus and Arabia, he went up to Jerusalem to get to know Peter, and he stayed with him for fifteen days.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia to defend the claim that the gospel he preaches came directly from Christ, not from human leaders. That is why he details his movements: he did not rush to seek the approval of the apostles. The three years are counted either from his conversion or from his return to Damascus; commentators do not agree on which. What is not stated is what they talked about during those fifteen days.

For today: value the counsel and fellowship of mature believers, but let your faith rest on Christ himself. Learn from others with humility, without depending on them to believe.
exp.0:20:
Paul says that, after his visit to Jerusalem, he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. These are areas north of Judea, in what would today be the southeast of Turkey and Syria.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia to defend that the gospel he preaches he received from Jesus Christ, not from men. For this reason he details his movements: he had almost no contact with the apostles in Jerusalem. In this way he shows that his message did not depend on them. Some believe that his hometown, Tarsus, was in Cilicia, but the text does not say so here.

God can shape a person in quiet, little-seen places, far from applause. If today you feel you are in a hidden or slow season, do not think that time is being wasted. Keep being faithful and learning from God, because He also works in the silent processes.
exp.1:0:
Paul says that, after fourteen years, he went back up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and also took Titus with him. The words "I went up again" show that he had already been there before. The fourteen years are counted from his conversion or from his first visit; scholars interpret this in different ways.

Paul is speaking in his letter to the churches of Galatia. He argues that the gospel he preaches did not come from men but from God. He mentions this visit to show that his message to the Gentiles was the same as that of the apostles. Titus, a Greek believer, would be a living proof of that truth.

For today: we do not need to add human requirements to the grace of God. Even so, it is wise to share what we believe with other mature believers, so that we walk in unity and do not run in vain.
exp.1:2:
It says that Titus, Paul's companion, was a Greek, meaning he was not Jewish, and yet no one forced him to be circumcised. Circumcision was the sign of the law of Moses for Jewish men.

Paul speaks here in his letter to the Galatians. He tells of his visit to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, to set out the gospel before the leaders. Titus was a living example: a believer who was not Jewish and was accepted without being required to be circumcised. Paul argues that salvation is by grace, not by adding requirements from the law. Some commentators debate whether Titus was or was not pressured; the text says he was not compelled.

For today: let us not add human rules to the grace of Christ. Let us welcome others because of their faith in Jesus, without demanding extra requirements before they feel accepted.
exp.1:5:
Paul speaks about the leaders of the church in Jerusalem, the ones who had a reputation for being important. He says that whatever they were before does not matter to him, because God does not look at outward appearance or at a person's standing. He adds that those leaders did not add anything to his message.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia to defend the gospel of grace. Some were saying that his message came secondhand and needed the approval of Jerusalem. Paul tells how he met with them, but that they did not correct his message; on the contrary, they recognized his calling to the non-Jewish peoples. He does not say this with contempt toward them, but to defend the truth.

Today we can learn not to measure faith by someone's fame, position, or popularity. It is good to examine every teaching in the light of God's Word, and to remember that he looks at the heart.
exp.1:8:
Paul tells how James, Cephas (Peter) and John, who were regarded as "pillars" of the church, recognized the grace God had given him. So they gave their right hands to him and to Barnabas as a sign of fellowship and agreement. Thus Paul and Barnabas would go to the Gentiles (the non-Jews), and they would go to those of the circumcision (the Jews).

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia and defends that his message comes from God. He tells that the leaders in Jerusalem added nothing to the gospel, but approved his calling. This shows unity in what is essential, even though each one had a different field of work.

For today: value other believers who serve differently from you. There is no need to compete. If God has called them and their fruit is evident, give them your hand and work together for the same gospel.
exp.1:9:
The only thing the leaders in Jerusalem asked of Paul was that he not forget the poor. And Paul says that this very thing was what he was already eagerly working to do. "Eager" here means diligent, willing, and attentive.

Paul speaks of this in his letter to the Galatians. He tells how James, Peter, and John accepted his message and his mission to the non-Jews without adding requirements. There was only this one request. Many understand it to refer to the poor among the believers in Jerusalem, although the text does not specify this. Paul mentions it to show that the gospel of grace and generosity go together.

For today: true faith shows itself in practical care for those in need. Think of a person or family close to you who is in need, and help them this week with something concrete.
exp.2:0:
Paul says to the Galatians: "How foolish you are! Who has put a spell on you, so that you no longer obey the truth?" He reminds them that Jesus Christ was clearly presented to them as crucified among them. The word "foolish" means without understanding, and "bewitched" means put a spell on or deceived.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, concerned that some teachers were telling them that, in addition to believing in Christ, they had to keep the law of Moses to be accepted by God. He speaks with firmness, but with the pain of a pastor who loves his people. Scholars debate exactly where these churches were, but the central message is clear.

For today: when you feel tempted to earn God's love through effort and rules, look again at the cross. There Christ did what you could not do.
exp.2:1:
Paul asks the Galatians one simple question: how did you receive the Spirit? Was it by doing the works of the law of Moses, or by hearing the message of the gospel and believing it? The "you" here is plural, meaning all of them together, and "hearing with faith" means listening to the message of Christ and trusting it.

Paul writes firmly to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, in addition to believing in Jesus, they had to keep the law in order to be accepted by God. Paul reminds them of their own experience: they had already received the Spirit when they believed, without doing works of the law. His question is meant to help them recognize what God had already done.

For today: do not spend your life trying to earn God's love through your own efforts. Trust in Christ every day, and let his Spirit transform you.
exp.2:9:
Galatians 3:10 says that those who rely on keeping the law to be accepted by God are under a curse. Paul quotes Scripture: cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things the law requires, to do them. "Curse" means condemnation or punishment from God. "Continue" means to keep on steadily. The law demands complete obedience, not partial obedience.

Paul is writing to the Galatians, who were being pressured to add the works of the law to faith in Christ. He quotes Deuteronomy 27:26. His argument is that no one keeps everything, so the law cannot save. That is why he insists that the blessing promised to Abraham comes through faith.

For today: do not try to earn God's favor through good behavior. Humbly acknowledge your failures, trust in Christ, and then obey out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.2:13:
He says that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law for a double purpose: so that the blessing promised to Abraham would also come to the non-Jews (the "Gentiles"), and so that all of us, through faith, would receive the promised Holy Spirit.

The apostle Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some wanted the believers who were not Jewish to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. Paul answers that the blessing never came through obeying the law, but through faith, just as it did with Abraham. Christ bore the curse so that this path would be open to us.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love by your efforts or by your background. Trust in Christ, and rest in the knowledge that God's Spirit is a gift received by faith, not a reward for behaving well.
exp.2:18:
Paul asks a question that anyone would ask: if God's promise to Abraham was already enough, then what is the law for? He answers that it was added because of transgressions. This can be understood in two ways: that the law made the sins visible, or that it restrained them. It lasted until the seed should come, who is Christ. It was ordained through angels and handed down by means of a mediator, which is understood to be Moses.

Paul is writing to the Galatians, who were being persuaded that they had to keep the law in order to be righteous before God. He makes clear that the law does not cancel the promise, but serves a temporary purpose.

For today: when you see your failures, let them lead you to Christ and not to despair. Rest in God's promise, not in your own performance.
exp.2:19:
It says that a mediator always acts between two parties, not just one. By contrast, God is one. Here "mediator" refers to the one who stood between God and the people when the law was given (Moses, according to most readers). This verse is famous for being difficult, and it has been interpreted in many ways.

Paul is writing to the Galatians, who were tempted to depend on the law to be accepted by God. He explains that the law came through angels and through a mediator, with two parties involved. The promise to Abraham, by contrast, came directly from God, who gave it by his grace alone. For that reason the promise carries more weight and is not nullified by the law.

For today: rest in what God promised and did for you in Christ, and not in your performance. Serve God with gratitude, not to earn his love.
exp.2:24:
What it says: Paul explains that, now that faith in Christ has come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster. In that time, the schoolmaster was a guide or tutor, often a trusted slave, who looked after and disciplined the child until he grew up. Here the schoolmaster is the law.

Context: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some wanted to return to keeping the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He answers that the law had a temporary role: to lead us to Christ. Now, through faith, all of us are children of God.

For today: Do not live trying to earn God's love through lists of rules or achievements. Rules can guide you, but your identity rests in Christ. Obey as a beloved child, not as someone who fears being rejected.
exp.2:25:
This verse says that all believers are children of God, not because they keep the law or because they belong to a people, but because they trust in Christ Jesus. A guide or tutor is someone who looked after children until they grew up.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia. Some were teaching them that, to be fully part of God's people, they had to follow the law of Moses. Paul answers that the law was like a guardian who prepared the way toward Christ. Now that faith has come, everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, enters God's family in the same way.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through effort or compare yourself with others. If you trust in Christ, you are already a son or daughter of God. Live with that assurance, and treat other believers as brothers and sisters, regardless of their background or condition.
exp.2:28:
This verse says that whoever belongs to Christ is also a descendant of Abraham. Therefore, according to the promise God made to Abraham, that person is an heir. "Seed" means descendants, and an "heir" is someone who receives what was promised to them.

Paul writes to the Christians in Galatia, where some were teaching that one had to keep the law of Moses to be part of God's people. Paul answers that faith in Christ is enough. He had already said that in Christ all are one, regardless of origin, social standing, or sex. Here he concludes that this union with Christ gives a share in the promise made to Abraham.

For today: you do not need to earn your place through merit or compare yourself with others. If you trust in Christ, you already belong to God's family. Treat your brothers and sisters in the faith as equals, regardless of their background or position.
exp.3:1:
He says that a child who is heir, although he is owner of everything, lives under the care of guardians (those who lead and watch over him) and managers (those who administer his property). This lasts until the date his father has already set. In the meantime, he is like a servant, because he does not command or decide.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were tempted to return to the law as a way to please God. He uses a scene common in his time to show that the law had a temporary role, until God sent his Son. Scholars debate details of the legal customs Paul had in mind, but the central idea is clear.

For today: if you are a child of God through Christ, do not live with the fear of a servant. Trust that God knows the times of your growing, and walk with the freedom and responsibility of a son.
exp.3:13:
Paul reminds the Galatians that, although he had a physical trial that could have led them to reject him, they did not despise him. On the contrary, they welcomed him with honor, as a messenger sent by God, even as Christ himself.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were now being led astray by false teachers. He reminds them of the affection they once had so that they can see how much they have changed. We do not know for certain what his illness was; some think of a problem with his eyes, but this is not certain.

Today we can learn to value people for the message of God they bring and not for their appearance or their weaknesses. We can also be thankful to those who taught us the faith, and not forget the love with which we once received the truth.
exp.3:20:
Paul asks the Galatians a direct question. They wanted to live "under the law," that is, under Moses' system of rules, in order to be accepted by God. Paul asks them whether they have truly listened to what the law itself teaches, since they defend it but do not understand its full message.

Paul writes with the heart of a father, concerned and even deeply troubled for them. Some teachers were telling them they must add the law to faith in Christ. That is why Paul uses the law itself, the account of Abraham, to show them that God's promise travels another road: the road of faith.

For today: before you burden yourself with rules to earn God's favor, listen again to what his Word says about his grace. Rest in what Christ has already done.
exp.3:21:
Paul recalls a fact found in Scripture: Abraham had two sons. One was born to a bondmaid, that is, a female slave (Hagar, who gave birth to Ishmael). The other was born to the freewoman (Sarah, mother of Isaac). The words "it is written" indicate that this comes from the Old Testament.

Paul is writing to Christians in Galatia who were drawn to living under the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He is concerned for them and asks whether they have really listened to what the law says. He uses the story of Abraham as an illustration, and in the verses that follow he explains it as an allegory, that is, a picture with a deeper meaning.

For today: you do not need to earn God's love through efforts and rules. Live as a free child, trusting in God's promise and in what Christ has done for you.
exp.3:23:
Paul says that the story of Hagar and Sarah has a deeper meaning. An allegory means that real events also serve as a picture of another teaching. The two women represent two covenants, or agreements God makes with his people. Hagar, the servant, is connected with Mount Sinai, where the law was given, and her children are born to bondage, that is, slavery.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being pressured to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He uses this well-known story to show that depending on the law leads to a life of slavery, while God's promise brings freedom.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through effort and lists of rules. Trust in the promise of Christ and live with gratitude, as a free child.
exp.3:26:
She says that the barren woman, the one who had no children and was forsaken, should rejoice and cry out with joy, because she will have more children than the one who has a husband.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were tempted to return to the law of Moses to be accepted by God. He quotes Isaiah 54:1, a promise to Jerusalem in exile, and applies it to the Jerusalem above, the mother of believers. Sarah, though barren, bore Isaac, the child of the promise. Paul wants to show that God's family is born through the promise and not through human effort.

For today: if you feel empty or without fruit, remember that God can give life where you see no way out. Trust in his promise and not in your own strength.
exp.4:0:
It says that we should stay firm in the freedom that Christ gave us. Paul asks us not to go back under that burden.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, besides believing in Christ, they had to keep the law of Moses, above all circumcision, in order to be accepted by God. Paul replies that trusting in that takes away the value of Christ's work. The verses that follow make this clear.

Today we can fall into thinking that God accepts us because of our works, rules, or efforts. This week, when you feel guilt or pressure to earn God's love, remember that Christ has already made you free. Rest in his grace and obey out of love, not out of fear.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that believers, guided by the Holy Spirit, eagerly wait with confidence for the hope of being declared righteous before God, and that this comes through faith, not through our own efforts. "Wait" here means to await with certainty. "Righteousness" refers to being accepted as righteous before God.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, to please God, they had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul answers them firmly: whoever seeks to be made righteous by the law has fallen away from grace. Against that, he affirms that believers live differently: by the Spirit and by faith in Christ.

For today: do not live trying to earn God's favor with lists of merits. Rest in what Christ has done, and ask the Spirit to sustain you as you wait patiently and confidently for what God has promised.
exp.4:6:
The explanation says that the believers in Galatia were doing very well in their Christian life, like a runner moving forward with strength. But someone hindered them, and Paul asks who stopped them so that they no longer obey the truth of the gospel.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, besides believing in Christ, they had to keep the law, such as circumcision. Paul is concerned and speaks with firmness, but also with the pain of a pastor. He reminds them that what counts is the faith that works through love. Scholars debate exactly who those teachers were, but the central problem is clear.

For today: think about who or what has hindered your walk with God. It may be a teaching that adds burdens to the gospel, or a voice that takes away your freedom in Christ. Return to the simple truth: God receives you by faith, and that faith shows itself in love.
exp.4:7:
What it says: Paul states that the way of thinking that pulled the Galatians away from the truth does not come from God, who is the one who calls them. The word "persuasion" in the verse refers to the conviction or influence that makes you change your mind. "The one who calls you" refers to God.

Context: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were listening to teachers saying that, in addition to believing in Christ, they had to be circumcised and keep the law to be accepted. Paul, with the tone of a worried pastor, reminds them that they started well and asks who stopped them. His answer is clear: that teaching did not come from God.

For today: When a teaching pulls you away from grace and from faith that works through love, test it against the Bible and ask yourself whether it truly comes from God. Not every convincing voice is the voice of the one who called you.
exp.4:12:
He says that God called us to be free, that is, free from trying to earn his favor by keeping rules such as circumcision. But that freedom is not permission to do whatever selfishness asks. Giving the flesh an opportunity means giving a pretext or an open door to selfish desires. Instead, Paul says that we should serve one another through love.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some teachers insisted that believers had to be circumcised to be accepted by God. Paul maintains that Christ, on the cross, already gave us freedom. But he also warns that this freedom can be twisted and cause quarrels among brothers and sisters, as the following verse shows.

For today: before deciding something you can do, ask yourself whether it will help or harm someone close to you. Use your freedom to serve, for example, by quietly helping someone who needs it this week.
exp.4:14:
It says that if believers bite and devour one another, like animals fighting, they will end up destroying each other. The images of biting and devouring describe fighting, harsh criticism, and mistreatment. Being consumed means to be finished off or wiped out.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He speaks to them about the freedom they have in Christ, but warns them not to use it for selfishness. It seems there were divisions and arguments among them, and the apostle reminds them that love for one's neighbor sums up the law. Right after this, he calls them to walk in the Spirit.

For today: before criticizing or responding in anger to a brother or sister, stop and ask yourself whether your words build up or tear down. Ask the Spirit to help you speak with love and seek peace.
exp.4:17:
This verse says that if the Holy Spirit is the one guiding us, we are no longer living under the law. "Led" means carried along, guided by the hand. "Under the law" means living under its demand and its condemnation, like someone trying to earn God's approval by keeping rules.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being pressured to return to the obligations of the law of Moses. He shows them that the Christian life is not sustained by rules, but by walking in the Spirit, who gives us strength to resist the sinful desires of the flesh. The verses that follow describe those works of the flesh.

For today: before deciding something, or when you feel tempted, pray and ask for the Spirit's guidance. Do not live only to check off a list, nor to do whatever you feel like. Seek a daily relationship with God, and let Him shape your character.
exp.4:21:
The explanation says that the Holy Spirit produces a fruit in the life of the believer, just as a healthy tree produces good fruit. It names love (here the word means generous love), joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, and faithfulness, which here can be understood as reliability or trust. It is "fruit" in the singular: one character with several sides.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, which were dividing and tearing at one another. He has just listed the works of the flesh, and now he contrasts them with what the Spirit brings forth in those who belong to him. His point is that the Christian life is not sustained by force of rules, but by the work of the Spirit in us.

For today: instead of only trying to control your bad temper or your impatience, ask the Spirit to change you from within. Pray each morning and choose one quality, such as patience, to practice that day.
exp.4:22:
This verse closes the list of the fruit of the Spirit with two qualities: meekness and temperance. Meekness is strength under control, a gentle character that does not seek to dominate. Temperance is self-control, knowing how to say no to disordered impulses. Then Paul adds that against such things there is no law: no one could condemn a life like this.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who felt pressured to live under the law of Moses. He shows them that the Spirit produces in the believer a character that the law aimed for but could not give. Earlier he had mentioned the works of the flesh, and now he presents the contrast.

For today: when you become angry or are tempted toward excess, before reacting, pause and ask the Spirit for calm and self-control. It is a fruit that God grows over time, not something you achieve by willpower alone.
exp.4:24:
If we have received new life from the Holy Spirit, this verse says, we should also let his guidance shape the way we live day to day. "Live" refers to the spiritual life that God gives. "Walk" means that our daily conduct should keep the same pace as the Spirit.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the churches in Galatia. Earlier he spoke of the fruit of the Spirit, such as gentleness and self-control, and of those who have put to death the flesh, that is, who have stopped obeying their selfish desires. Then he warns against conceit, provoking others, and envy. In this way Paul wants faith to be visible in how we treat other people.

For today: before you react with anger or envy, stop and pray. Ask yourself, "What would someone guided by the Spirit do here?" Then take one concrete step of patience or kindness.
exp.5:0:
If a fellow believer is caught doing something wrong, the text says that those who live guided by the Spirit should help him get back up, treating him kindly and with humility. "Caught" means found out or trapped in an error. "Restore" is like putting back in its proper place something that has been broken. "Gentleness" means kindness. And "tempted" means tested or put to the trial. It also warns each person to watch over himself, because he too could fall.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the churches of Galatia. He teaches them to live in freedom through the Spirit, without fighting among themselves. The verses that follow speak of carrying one another's burdens and of not thinking oneself superior.

Today, if someone close to you stumbles, do not judge or expose him. Speak to him in private, with affection and patience, remembering that you too need grace.
exp.5:7:
This verse uses the image of sowing and reaping. A person who sows to their own flesh, that is, who lives for their desires and selfishness, will reap decay, something that spoils and ends in ruin. A person who sows to the Spirit, that is, who lives guided by God, will reap life that never ends.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Galatia. He has just asked them to support those who teach them the word, and he warns them that God cannot be mocked. He reminds them that our choices have consequences. What follows encourages them not to grow weary of doing good.

For today: think about one small decision you make this week, such as how you use your time, your money, or your words. Ask yourself whether it is a seed for your own desires or for the Spirit. Choose one concrete action today, such as praying, forgiving, or helping someone, and do not lose heart if the harvest takes time.
exp.5:9:
As long as we have the opportunity, the verse says, we should do good to all people, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith, meaning the other believers who are members of God's family.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being pressured to return to the law. Just before this, he encouraged them not to grow weary of doing good, because there will be a harvest in due time. This verse applies that idea: the Christian life shows itself in concrete acts of love, first within the church and also toward everyone.

Today you can choose a specific person, from your church or your surroundings, and help them this week with something simple: a visit, a meal, a phone call, or a favor. Do it without expecting anything in return.
exp.5:12:
They say that those who pressure the Galatians to be circumcised do not even keep the whole law themselves. What they want is to boast, that is, to take pride that they succeeded in getting others to follow their practice. "Flesh" here refers to the body marked by circumcision, an outward sign.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being influenced by teachers who required circumcision in order to be accepted by God. Paul corrects them firmly, and he himself writes this part in his own hand, with large letters. He maintains that salvation is found in the cross of Christ, not in outward rites.

For today: examine your motives. It is easy to want others to follow our religious customs so that we feel superior. Instead, let your pride rest only in what Christ did for you on the cross, and treat others with humility and grace.
exp.5:13:
Paul says that he will never take pride in anything except the cross of Jesus Christ. Where a sentence would explain an unusual word, I have instead spoken of the boasting itself: to take pride or boast in something. In this verse, the word that presses or compels people is replaced with a plain description: some teachers were pressing the believers to be circumcised. Through that cross, the world with its values lost its power over Paul, and he also stopped being tied to that world.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were pressing non-Jewish believers to be circumcised, so that they would look good before others and avoid rejection. Paul answers that it is not about outward marks or about boasting in religious achievements. What counts is the new creation that God makes in the one who trusts in Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves what we tend to boast about: success, image, good religious behavior. We can hand over that need for approval and rest in what Christ has done for us, letting his love be our greatest confidence.
exp.5:14:
For those united with Christ, outward religious marks are not what matters most. Being circumcised or not does not change our standing before God. What counts is the new creation, that is, a new life that God himself produces in the person.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being pressured by some to be circumcised in order to be accepted by God. Paul replies that we should not boast in rituals, but only in the cross of Christ. Through it, their old way of living and of valuing things comes to an end.

For today: do not measure your faith by customs, titles, or religious appearances. Ask God to keep renewing your heart and your way of treating others.
exp.5:15:
Paul wishes peace and mercy on everyone who lives by this rule. This rule is what he has just said: what matters is not circumcision, but being a new creation in Christ. Living by this rule means living in a certain way, guided by it day after day. Mercy is God's compassion toward us.

Paul writes this letter to the churches of Galatia, where some teachers insisted that believers had to be circumcised and follow the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. As he closes the letter, Paul sums up his message: only the cross of Christ makes us new. The phrase "the Israel of God" is understood in different ways: many believe it refers to all believers, both Jews and Gentiles; others think it points to Jewish believers in particular.

Today, instead of measuring ourselves by outward rules or by comparisons, we can live each day trusting in what Christ did on the cross, and so receive his peace and his mercy.
exp.5:16:
He says that from now on no one should cause him trouble or bother him, because Paul carries in his body the "marks" of Jesus. The word "marks" (in Greek, stigmata) referred to signs or scars, like the brands that masters placed on their slaves.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some wanted to make circumcision a requirement for being accepted by God. He had already suffered beatings and persecution for preaching Christ (Acts 14:19; 2 Corinthians 11:23-25). Many believe he is referring to those scars, although the Bible does not spell this out. With this he closes the discussion: his life already shows whom he belongs to.

For today: what proves our faith is not arguments or religious appearances, but a life given to Christ, even when it costs. Live in such a way that others can see whom you belong to.
exp.2:22:
Here Paul says that before faith in Christ came, we were held in custody under the law, locked up until faith should be revealed. Paul is describing how the law kept people under guard and watch while the coming of Christ was being prepared.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were teaching that people had to keep the law of Moses in order to be righteous before God. He answers that the law is not against God's promises, but it cannot give life. Its task was to show sin and point toward Christ, like a guardian, that is, a guide who looks after a child until he grows up.

Today we can be thankful that God accepts us because we trust in Jesus, not because we keep a list of rules. Rules can guide us, but only Christ gives us life and freedom.
exp.3:10:
Paul says that he is afraid for the Galatians. He writes "I fear for you," meaning he is deeply concerned for them. He fears that all his effort in preaching to them, teaching them, and caring for them may have been wasted, that it may have come to nothing.

Paul writes to Christians in Galatia who came to know God through the gospel, but who were now returning to religious practices such as keeping days, months, and years, as if that would make them acceptable before God. Paul calls these practices "weak and beggarly elements": things that are weak and cannot save. He speaks with the pain of a father, not with coldness.

For today: if you notice that your faith is filling up with rules and outward appearances, return to what is essential: God knows you and loves you by grace in Christ. And if someone is drifting away, pray for that person and speak to them with kindness and truth.
exp.3:24:
Paul says that Hagar, Abraham's servant, stands for the covenant of the law given at Mount Sinai, in Arabia. The word "corresponds to" means "lines up with." So Hagar and Sinai are linked to the present-day Jerusalem, which lives under the law, enslaved along with its children.

Paul writes to the believers in Galatia, who were pressured to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He uses the story of Abraham as an allegory: the son of the servant was born "after the flesh," and the son of the free woman was born through God's promise.

Today, do not live as someone who must earn God's love through effort and performance. In Christ you are a free son; obey with gratitude, not with fear.
exp.2:4:
Paul asks the Galatians a direct question: God lavishes his Spirit on you and works miracles among you. Does he do this because you practice the law, or because you hear and believe?

The phrase "hear and believe" means listening to the gospel and trusting in it.

Paul writes this letter to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, in addition to believing in Christ, they had to keep the law, and Paul corrects that mistake. He reminds them of what they already experienced: they received the Spirit when they believed, not through their own effort. Afterward he will use Abraham as an example.

Today we can remember that our relationship with God begins and grows through trusting in Christ, not through trying to earn his favor. When you feel tired of trying to be enough, listen again to the gospel and rest in his grace.
exp.4:2:
Paul says that once again he gives a serious and solemn declaration to every man who chooses to be circumcised. Here "testify" means to state something with seriousness, not to complain. The warning is clear: whoever gets circumcised in order to be accepted by God becomes obligated to obey the whole law, not just part of it.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, to be fully part of God's people, non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised and keep the law. Paul answers that this changes where their trust lies: instead of resting on Christ, it becomes their own effort. It would mean going back to a yoke that no one can carry completely.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are adding rules or achievements to feel accepted by God. Rest in what Christ has done for you. From that freedom, serve others with love and gratitude, not with fear or in order to earn approval.
exp.2:14:
Paul speaks to his brothers and sisters and says he will put the matter in human terms. Even a human covenant, once it has been ratified, cannot be canceled or amended. In other words, a binding agreement between people stays in force, and no one can take it back or add to it. All the more, then, this holds true for what God has promised.

Paul was writing to Christians in Galatia who were being influenced to believe they had to add the works of the law in order to be accepted by God. For this reason he reminds them that the promise made to Abraham was already firmly established, and that the law came later and could not change it.

For today: you can rest in the fact that God's salvation and promises depend on his faithfulness, not on your achievements. Trust in Christ, and do not take on burdens that God has not placed on you.
exp.4:18:
Paul says that the acts of the flesh are obvious. He names three here: sexual immorality (sex outside the boundaries God sets, including sex outside of marriage), impurity (a dirty or corrupt way of living), and debauchery (living without restraint, given over to unchecked pleasure).

The word "flesh" here does not mean the body, but our human nature leaning toward sin.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He teaches them that following Christ does not mean returning to the law as a way to be saved, but it also does not mean living without limits. Earlier he explained that the flesh and the Spirit struggle against each other, and that whoever is guided by the Spirit lives differently.

For today: it is not enough to say "I don't want to sin." Each day, ask God to guide you by his Spirit, and stay away from whatever feeds your harmful desires. God gives you strength to change.
exp.2:21:
The Scripture pronounces all things confined by sin, meaning it shows that every person is held captive under sin and cannot free themselves by their own effort. The purpose was that the promise would be given to those who believe, and this comes through faith in Jesus Christ.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being tempted to add the law of Moses to faith in Christ. He asks whether the law is against God's promises, and he answers that it is not. But the law could never give life; its role was to show that all of us need a Savior. The promise to Abraham is received by faith.

Today you can rest in the knowledge that your relationship with God does not depend on your good performance. Acknowledge your failures with humility and trust in Christ. That faith frees you from living in fear or from comparing yourself with others.
exp.5:2:
If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. This verse says that if someone believes they are important or better than others, when in reality they are not, they are deceiving themselves. "Thinks he is something" means that a person believes they are someone significant, and "deceives himself" means that they fall into their own self-deception.

Paul writes to the churches in Galatia. He has just asked that those who are spiritual restore with gentleness someone who has fallen into a fault, and that they help carry one another's burdens. Here he warns that pride gets in the way of that help, because a person who feels superior looks down on others and does not restore them with meekness.

Today, before you correct or judge someone, ask yourself honestly: "Do I think I am better than this person?" Ask God for humility, remember that you too can stumble, and offer help with respect and affection.
exp.3:28:
At that time, the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit. It is the same now.

The explanation says that, just as Ishmael, the son born by ordinary human means, persecuted Isaac, the son born by God's promise, the same thing is happening now.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some teachers wanted believers to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. Paul uses the story of Hagar and Sarah as an illustration: whoever trusts in their own efforts is like the son of the slave woman, and whoever trusts in the promise is like Isaac. Genesis describes Ishmael mocking Isaac, and Paul understands this as persecution.

For today, do not be surprised if living by grace brings you criticism, even from religious people. Rest in the fact that you are a child of God through his promise, not through your own merits, and respond with patience and love.
exp.1:14:
We are Jews by birth, not Gentile sinners, Paul says. "By birth" means Jews by nature, not people who became Jews later by conversion. The phrase "Gentile sinners" was a common way among Jews of speaking about non-Jews, whom they regarded as outside the law of God.

Paul speaks to Peter in Antioch, in front of everyone. Peter had stopped eating with Gentile believers out of fear of other Jews. Paul begins with what both of them shared as Jews, and right away shows that they too were justified not by the law, but by faith in Christ.

For today: no background, tradition, or good record makes us right before God. If Christ received us by pure grace, let us treat others with that same acceptance, without making anyone feel inferior.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that God made promises to Abraham and to his offspring, that is, to his descendants. Paul points out that the Scripture does not say "and to seeds," meaning many, but "and to your seed," meaning one, who is Christ. The word "seed" in the verse means offspring or descendant, and the promises were spoken, meaning God gave them.

Paul writes to the believers in Galatia, who were being influenced to think they had to keep the law in order to be accepted by God. He reminds them that the promise came first, and that a covenant once confirmed is not changed. His argument follows the way he understood the text of Genesis; some scholars see it as a reading of Christ as the head of a people, not only as an individual.

For today: your relationship with God rests on what Christ did, not on your performance. Rest in his promise and respond with gratitude.
exp.2:8:
This verse says that the people who trust God receive God's blessing together with Abraham. Their blessing is not something they earned, but something they receive as believers. Abraham is called "the man of faith" because he believed what God told him.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Galatia, who were being influenced to think that they had to keep the law of Moses in order to please God. Paul reminds them that God had already promised to bless all the nations through Abraham, long before the law existed. Therefore, the blessing comes through faith and not through one's own effort.

Today you can rest in the fact that God accepts you because you trust in Christ, not because of your achievements. When you feel inadequate, trust again in his promise and live thankful, not afraid.
exp.3:25:
It says there is a Jerusalem "above," meaning a heavenly Jerusalem, and that she is free. Paul also calls her "our mother," meaning the mother of all who believe in Christ. The word "But" and the word "Jerusalem" appear here just as they do in the verse above.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being tempted to return to the law of Moses in order to feel accepted by God. He uses the story of Hagar and Sarah as an allegory. Hagar represents the covenant of Sinai and slavery; Sarah represents the promise and freedom. Paul wants to show that believers belong to the free family of God.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through effort or through fear. In Christ you are already a son or daughter, with a place in his family. Live thankfully, obeying him out of love and not in order to be accepted.
exp.2:17:
Paul says that God's inheritance cannot depend on two things at once. If the inheritance depends on the law, then it no longer depends on a promise. But God freely granted it to Abraham through a promise.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being pressured to rely on the law of Moses to be accepted by God. He had already explained that the promise came first, and that the law arrived 430 years later. For that reason, the law could not cancel what God had already promised.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through religious effort. Receive his gift in Christ with gratitude, and let that gratitude move your obedience, not fear.
exp.0:6:
Paul says there is really no other gospel, meaning no other true good news. What does exist are people who trouble you, unsettling you and filling you with confusion. They are trying to distort the gospel, twisting and changing it until it becomes something different from what it is.

Paul writes to the churches in Galatia. He is amazed that they are turning away so quickly from the grace they received. From the rest of the letter, it is clear that these teachers were adding requirements to faith in Christ. Scholars debate the exact details of that group, but the central problem was changing the message of grace.

Today, when we hear a teaching, let us compare it with what the Bible says about Jesus. If it adds burdens or takes away grace, it is wise to examine it calmly, with prayer and with other mature believers.
exp.5:10:
See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand! Paul asks the Galatians to take notice of how big the letters are, since he is writing this part himself. "See" here means "look" or "pay attention." Up to this point, someone else may have been writing down the letter, and now Paul takes up the pen himself.

Paul is writing to the churches of Galatia, who were being pressed to be circumcised in order to be accepted by God. At the end of the letter, he writes in his own hand to give weight to his words. Scholars debate why the letters were large: some think it was for emphasis, others that he had poor eyesight, but the Bible does not make it clear.

Today, when something is very important, it is worth saying it clearly and sincerely, without beating around the bush. And we can also listen closely to what is essential: that Christ is enough, and that doing good springs from that faith.
exp.3:29:
Paul asks what the Scripture says, and he quotes the words spoken about Hagar and Ishmear in Genesis: "Expel the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman's son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman's son." The slave woman is Hagar and her son is Ishmael. The slave woman's son will not share the inheritance with Isaac, the son of the free woman, Sarah.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being pressured to return to the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He uses the story of Abraham as an illustration: Ishmael was born through human effort, and Isaac through God's promise (Genesis 21:10). For Paul, the inheritance comes through the promise, not through works. Some interpreters debate the details of this allegory, but its central point is clear.

For today: do not try to earn God's love through efforts or merits. Rest in his promise, and let go of everything that makes you feel enslaved to guilt or to appearances.
exp.3:0:
Paul says that an heir, as long as he is still a child, is no different from a slave, even though he is in fact the owner of everything his father has. Everything belongs to him, but in practice he lives under rules and cannot decide anything about his inheritance.

Paul writes to the churches in Galatia, who were drawn toward returning to the law of Moses as a requirement for being accepted by God. He uses this everyday picture to show that the time under the law was a stage of preparation, until Christ came. Scholars debate exactly what is meant by the elementary forces of the world, but the central point is clear: that stage has already passed.

Today, if you trust in Christ, you are a child of God and not a fearful servant. Live with the confidence of a beloved child, not trying to earn God's affection through religious effort.
exp.1:17:
He says that if someone rebuilds what they once tore down, they prove themselves to be a lawbreaker.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being pressed to add the law of Moses to faith in Christ. Earlier he had explained in Antioch that people are made right with God through faith, not through works of the law. Here he speaks in the first person as an example. Interpreters debate exactly what was "torn down," but the general sense is that he had given up the law as a way to be accepted by God. Going back to it would contradict himself.

For today: do not return to trying to earn God's love through your good behavior. Obey out of gratitude, resting in what Christ has already done for you.
exp.0:11:
Paul says that the gospel he preaches did not come to him from any human being, and that no one taught it to him. Instead, he received it through a revelation from Jesus Christ, meaning that Jesus himself made it known to him. The word "revelation" means that God uncovers something that could not be seen before.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some teachers were saying that his message was secondhand and needed correcting. He insists that his message of salvation by grace does not come from human opinions. He then recalls his former life as a persecutor, to show that his change can be explained only by God's action. Scholars debate when and how this revelation happened, but Paul ties it to his encounter with Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith rests on customs, popular opinions, or on Jesus himself. Let us read the Gospels with humility and ask God to teach us to know him truly.
exp.0:1:
This verse completes the letter's greeting. Paul writes to "the churches of Galatia" along with "all the brothers with me." The verse does not say who these brothers were or how many there were.

Paul is the one speaking, and he has just argued that his calling as an apostle comes from God and not from people. Galatia was a region, which is why he speaks of several churches rather than one. Scholars debate the exact location where these believers lived, but the letter makes clear that Paul writes with concern and firmness.

For today: the Christian faith is not lived alone. Paul does not write by himself but alongside other brothers. Seek a community of believers to walk with you, and pray for it.
exp.0:23:
The explanation says that the people in the churches of Judea praised God because of what He had done in Paul. The word "glorified" means that they recognized God as the source of the change and gave Him honor. The verse can be read as "because of me," meaning they praised God on account of Paul's changed life, which is the same meaning that comes through when it is read as "because of what God did in me."

Paul writes in his letter to the Galatians. He argues that the gospel he preaches comes from God and not from the apostles in Jerusalem. He recounts that, after his conversion, he was not personally known to the churches of Judea. They only heard that the former persecutor was now proclaiming the faith. His transformation was so real that it caused gratitude, not distrust.

For today: when God changes your life, or someone else's, make sure the praise does not stop with you. Let your testimony lead others to give thanks to God, and rejoice sincerely when He transforms a difficult person.
exp.5:17:
Paul closes his letter by wishing that the grace of Jesus Christ be with your spirit, that is, with the deepest part of each one of you. The words "your spirit" are addressed to all the readers together.

Paul is writing to the churches of Galatia, who were being pressed to depend on the law to be accepted by God. After firmly defending the truth that we are saved by grace, he ends with a warm blessing. He calls them "brothers," showing affection even after having corrected them sharply.

Today we can remember that grace is not only the beginning of faith but also the air we breathe each day. When you feel weary of striving to earn God's love, rest in his grace, and bless others with that same grace.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that the One who was at work in Peter's apostleship to the circumcised was also at work in Paul's apostleship to the Gentiles. God gave power to Peter for his work among the Jews and gave power to Paul for his work among the non-Jews. The phrase "at work in" means God was active in both of them.

Paul speaks to the Galatians and tells what happened when he met with the leaders in Jerusalem. Some were saying that his message was inferior or needed correction. Paul maintains that his calling did not come from men but from God, and that the leading apostles recognized it when they saw the fruits of his ministry.

For today: God calls different people to serve in different ways. Instead of comparing ourselves with others or belittling their service, we can recognize God's work in them and work together with humility in what He has entrusted to us.
exp.0:4:
All glory, that is, all honor and praise, belongs to God the Father, and it will be so forever. The phrase "forever and ever" means that this glory never ends. The word "Amen" means "so be it" or "we agree."

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He has just greeted them and reminded them that Jesus gave himself for our sins, according to the will of the Father. This praise flows out of his gratitude for that gift. Right away, Paul expresses his amazement that they are turning away from the gospel, and for this reason his whole letter defends that salvation is by grace.

For today: before we worry about our struggles or arguments, we can begin the day by praising God for what Christ has done. This reminds us that we do not earn salvation ourselves, and that all the glory belongs to God.
exp.2:10:
No one is made righteous before God by keeping the law. "Being justified" means being accepted and counted right with Him. Paul supports this with a line of Scripture: "The righteous will live by faith." In other words, true life with God comes through trusting Him, not through straining to keep rules.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some taught that, in order to please God, the law of Moses had to be added to faith in Christ. He answers that the law demanded perfect obedience in everything, and so it condemned anyone who did not achieve it. He cites Habakkuk 2:4 to show that faith has always been the way. Then he explains that Christ bore that curse for us.

Today, you do not have to earn God's love by your good behavior. Trust in Christ, rest in His forgiveness, and obey out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.0:10:
Paul tells the brothers in Galatia that he wants them to know something clearly: the gospel he preached was not devised by man. "Not devised by man" means it was not invented, made up, or adjusted by people.

Paul is writing to the churches of Galatia, who were being confused by those who taught a different message. Earlier he has said that he is not trying to please people, but to serve Christ. Now he defends that his message comes from God, and in the verses that follow he explains that he received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what we believe comes from the Word of God or from what is convenient, popular, or pleasing. It is worth returning to the Scriptures and measuring everything by what Christ has revealed.
exp.4:15:
Paul says that we should live guided by the Holy Spirit, and not give in to the wrong desires of our human nature. The verse's command to "walk" means to live day by day by the Spirit. The wrong desires he describes are strong longings for what is wrong. "Flesh" here does not mean the body, but our tendency to live for self and far from God.

Paul writes to the churches in Galatia. There were quarrels among them, and some wanted to go back to depending on the law to be accepted. He reminds them that love for one's neighbor sums up the law, and that biting and fighting destroy them. His answer is not more rules, but depending on the Spirit.

For today: when you feel anger, envy, or the urge to hurt someone, stop and pray: "Holy Spirit, guide me now." Then choose an act of love, such as answering calmly or asking forgiveness.
exp.1:4:
Here Paul says that he did not give in to the false brothers, not even for a moment. The phrase in the verse for "we did not give in" means that they did not submit or allow themselves to be pressured. His goal was that the truth of the gospel would remain firm among the Galatians, without being mixed with added requirements.

Paul writes in a letter to the churches of Galatia. He recounts what happened in Jerusalem, when some insisted that Titus, a Greek believer, be circumcised in order to be accepted. Paul saw in this an attempt to take away the freedom that is received in Christ, and so he stood firm.

For today: we can be kind to people, but we must not add rules or burdens to the message that we are saved by grace through faith in Christ. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern what is essential and what is not.
exp.5:1:
It says that believers should help one another carry their burdens. "Carry" means to hold up together, to help one another get through hard things. "Fulfill" means to put into practice. So, by helping others, one lives out what Christ taught.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Just before this, he speaks of gently restoring someone who has fallen into a fault. Then he warns against thinking oneself superior and asks that each person examine his own life. Many understand "the law of Christ" to refer to the love that Jesus commanded and lived, though some explain it in other ways.

Today you can notice someone close to you who is tired, sick, or going through a difficulty, and offer them something concrete: listening to them, praying with them, cooking for them, or accompanying them to an appointment. Truly helping starts with a simple step.
exp.5:5:
The explanation says that the one who receives instruction in God's Word must share in all good things with his teacher. "Share in" means to take part in or give a portion of something. "All good things" can include money, food, lodging and other material help, though some also think of broader support such as affection and cooperation.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Shortly before, he spoke of bearing one another's burdens and of each person examining his own work. Here he gives a concrete example of generosity. What follows, about sowing and reaping, suggests that giving is a sowing that God sees and rewards.

Today, we can support those who teach us the Bible with generosity and gratitude, whether through offerings, practical help or words of encouragement, without taking their work for granted.
exp.2:11:
What it says: The law does not work through trust in God, but through doing what it commands. Its principle is that whoever does these things will live by them. The law asks for doing, not only for believing.

Context: Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being pressured to add the law of Moses to their faith in Christ. He quotes Leviticus 18:5 to show that the law demands complete obedience, and that no one keeps it perfectly. That is why, he says, we are made right with God through faith, and Christ has freed us from the curse the law brings.

For today: Do not try to earn God's love by your good behavior. Trust in what Christ has already done for you, and let that gratitude lead you to obey him with joy, not with fear.
exp.4:3:
This explanation says that those who try to be declared right before God by keeping the law are cut off from Christ and so do not receive what He gives. "You who are trying to be justified" means seeking to be accepted by God. "Severed from Christ" means separated from Him, unable to receive His benefit. "Fallen away from grace" means they left the path of God's undeserved favor to rely on their own efforts.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were insisting that non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised and keep the law in order to be saved. Paul answers firmly: adding the law to Christ denies that Christ is enough. He then points out that hope lies in faith that works through love.

For today: do not try to earn God's favor through good works, religiousness, or perfection. Rest in Christ, and let your obedience come from love and gratitude.
exp.3:19:
Paul says he wishes he could be with the Galatians right now and change his tone. He is expressing a strong desire to be there in person. "Change my tone" means speaking to them in a different way, perhaps with more gentleness. "Perplexed about you" means he is confused and does not know what to think about them.

Paul writes to them like a worried father. The Galatians were giving up the freedom of the gospel to go back to depending on the law as a way of being made right with God. He calls them "my little children" and suffers for them as a mother does in childbirth. Because he is writing a letter, he cannot see their faces or judge how they are responding, and so he feels limited. Some scholars think he wanted to soften his tone; others think he wanted to speak to them with more firmness. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when someone you love goes astray, do not stay silent or treat them coldly. Speak with truth, but with the heart of a father or mother, asking God for wisdom to find the right tone.
exp.5:8:
It says that we should not grow weary of doing good, because in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up. "In due time" means "at the right moment." Reaping is harvesting, and the word translated as "weary" means worn out in strength or having given up.

The apostle Paul is speaking to the churches of Galatia. He has just explained that whatever a person sows, that they will reap: sowing for the flesh leads to ruin, and sowing for the Spirit leads to eternal life. With this in mind he encourages them to persevere, and then calls them to do good to everyone, especially to those of the household of faith.

For today: if you grow tired of helping, forgiving, or being steady in something good and you do not yet see results, do not give up. Choose one small good action, such as visiting someone or serving quietly, and keep at it, trusting that God takes care of the harvest.
exp.2:6:
Understand, then, that Abraham's true children are not those who are so by blood or by keeping the law, but those who trust God as he did. "Understand" means "recognize as certain," and in this verse the phrase "those who have faith" refers to people who live by trusting God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Galatia, who were being influenced by people who said that, to belong to God's people, they had to keep the law of Moses. Paul reminds them that they received the Spirit by believing, not by keeping rules. Abraham was declared righteous because of his faith, so God's family is recognized by faith.

Today we can rest in the fact that God accepts us because we trust in Christ, not because of our performance. This frees us from the pressure of earning his love and unites us with believers from every culture.
exp.4:16:
Within the believer there is a struggle. The "flesh" is our human nature, inclined toward selfishness and sin, and it craves what runs against the Spirit. The Spirit, in turn, desires what is opposed to the flesh. Because these two are set against each other, we do not always do what we want.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were quarreling among themselves and arguing about the law. He tells them to live led by the Spirit, not by the cravings of the flesh. Some understand the last part as describing the believer's frustration; others understand it as the Spirit keeping the flesh from getting its way. Both readings are possible.

Today, when you feel the pull to respond with anger or selfishness, pause and pray. Ask the Spirit to guide you to choose love.
exp.2:20:
Paul asks whether the law is opposed to the promises of God. He answers emphatically: "Certainly not!" He explains that if a law had been given that could impart life (to impart life means to make alive), then righteousness, that is, being accepted by God, would indeed have come from keeping it.

Paul writes to the Galatians, believers who were being pressured to add the law to faith in Christ. He makes clear to them that the law and the promise are not in competition: the law showed sin, but it could not save. Only the promise, received by faith, gives life.

For today: let us not trust in our good works to earn God's favor. Obeying him is good, but our security rests in Jesus Christ. Rest in his grace and obey with gratitude.
exp.0:2:
Paul wishes the believers in Galatia grace and peace. Grace is the undeserved favor of God, and peace is a settled tranquility and reconciliation with Him. Both come to them from two sources: God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul writes this letter to several churches in Galatia. Before this greeting, he has already made clear that his authority as an apostle comes from Jesus Christ and from God, not from men. This greeting is similar to the greetings in his other letters, but here it prepares the ground for correcting those who were turning away from the gospel.

For today: do not live trying to earn God's favor. Begin each day by remembering that His grace is already with you, and let that grace give you peace in the midst of your worries.
exp.4:8:
A small amount of yeast, which is what makes bread rise, ends up working through the whole batch of dough. The point is that something small can affect the whole.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were doing well in their faith, but some teachers were persuading them that they had to be circumcised to be accepted by God. Paul fears that this teaching, though it may seem minor, will spread and corrupt the truth of the gospel of grace. Interpreters debate whether the "leaven" is the false teaching or the people who teach it; both ideas fit the text.

Today, let us not take lightly ideas or small habits that drift away from the truth. Let us examine carefully what we hear, and let the grace of Christ be our foundation.
exp.4:13:
Paul says that the whole law of God is summed up and fulfilled in one sentence: to love your neighbor as yourself. The meaning of "neighbor" is anyone we have close to us, and "is fulfilled" means that the purpose of the law is accomplished through love.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Galatia, who were being pressured by teachers who wanted to impose the law of Moses on them. He reminds them that they were called to freedom, but that freedom is not for living selfishly; it is for serving one another through love. If they bite and devour each other, they will destroy one another.

Today we can ask ourselves before we act or speak: "Is this love toward the other person?" For example, instead of criticizing someone in church or in the family, we can choose to serve them with a concrete and patient act.
exp.4:20:
This verse ends the list of the "works of the flesh." Paul names envy, murder, drunkenness, and orgies (wild parties with excessive food and drink and uncontrolled behavior), along with similar things. Then he warns, as he did before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. The phrase "I warn you" here means "I solemnly declare."

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, which were confused and quarreling among themselves. He reminds them that Christian life is not lived by one's own effort or by the law, but guided by the Spirit. The verses that follow contrast these works with the fruit of the Spirit.

Today you might ask yourself: "What attitude dominates my life, such as envy or excess?" Bring it before God with sincerity and ask the Spirit to transform you. Cultivate love, peace, and self-control with God's help, not merely by willpower.
exp.1:16:
It says that if, while seeking to be declared righteous before God through Christ, we ourselves, even we Jews, are found to be sinners (like the Gentiles), does that make Christ a servant or promoter of sin? Paul answers firmly: "Certainly not!" That is, never! "Declared righteous" means being counted as righteous before God.

Paul is speaking to the Galatians and recalls what he said to Peter in Antioch. Some thought that leaving the law as a way to salvation led to living in sin. Scholars explain the exact meaning of "found to be sinners" in several ways, but Paul rejects the idea that Christ encourages sin.

For today: grace is not an excuse to sin. Trust in Christ to be righteous before God, and let that faith lead you to live in a way that pleases him.
exp.1:20:
Paul says that he does not reject or set aside the grace of God. Here, "set aside" means to treat as worthless or push away. Where the verse says "died for nothing," it means that his death would have had no purpose or necessity. If a person could be declared righteous before God by keeping the law, then the death of Christ would have been pointless.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some taught that, in addition to believing in Christ, a person had to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. Just before this, Paul explained that his life now is lived by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him. That is why he argues that adding works to grace despises it.

For today: do not try to earn the love of God through your good behavior. Rest in what Christ has already done for you, and let that love move you to live thankful and obedient.
exp.5:11:
It says that those who want to make a good impression outwardly are trying to compel the Galatians to be circumcised. They do this only to avoid persecution for the cross of Christ. The verse's word "compel" means to force or press hard.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers taught that non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised to be accepted by God. Paul says that they were seeking approval and security, and that they did not even keep the whole law themselves. He, on the other hand, boasts only in the cross of Christ.

For today: examine whether you sometimes stay silent or change your faith out of fear of rejection. Ask God for the courage to live out the message of the cross simply, with love, and without seeking applause.
exp.3:18:
Paul calls the believers in Galatia "my children" and says that he is once again in the pains of childbirth for them. Those pains will continue until Christ is formed in them, that is, until Christ's character and his way of life are truly seen in their lives. The word "until" marks the point when this will be complete, and the pains describe the deep and real effort a mother makes when she gives birth.

Paul writes this letter with real concern. Some teachers were telling them that, to be accepted by God, they had to add the law of Moses to faith in Christ. Paul, who had first brought them the gospel, feels like an anxious mother as he sees them turning away. His tone mixes tenderness and firmness.

For today: being a Christian is much more than keeping rules; it is letting Christ shape our hearts over time. We can pray for, and patiently and lovingly walk alongside, those who are growing in faith.
exp.2:23:
The explanation says that the law of Moses was like a "guardian," the guide or caretaker who looked after and disciplined a child until he grew up. Its purpose was to lead us to Christ, so that God would declare us righteous by faith, not by keeping rules.

Paul writes to the believers in Galatia, who were being pressured to add Jewish law to their faith in Jesus. He explains that the law had a temporary purpose: to show sin and point to the need for a Savior. Some understand "guardian" as a protector, others as a disciplinarian; both ideas fit.

For today: do not rely on your good behavior to be accepted by God. Let the awareness of your failings draw you closer to Christ, and live thankfully, resting in his grace.
exp.3:27:
It says that believers, like Isaac, are children of the promise. Isaac was born because God kept what he had promised to Abraham and Sarah, not through mere human effort. "Brothers" refers to the Christians of Galatia. "Promise" is what God said he would do, and he carries it out through his own faithfulness.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some wanted to require the law of Moses as the way to be accepted by God. He uses the story of Hagar and Sarah as a comparison: Ishmael was born through a human plan, and Isaac through the promise. With this, Paul shows that belonging to God comes through faith and his grace, not through works of the law. Interpreters debate some details of this comparison, but the central idea is clear.

Today you can rest in the knowledge that God received you by his promise and his grace, not by your performance. Live thankful, without fear of losing your place in his family.
exp.2:26:
Galatians 3:27 says that everyone who was baptized into Christ has clothed themselves with Christ. The phrase "were baptized" refers to the people you are addressing, and "have clothed yourselves" describes putting on Christ as if He were a garment. It is an image of identity: whoever trusts in Jesus is united with Him and stands before God in Him.

The apostle Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being pressured to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. Before, the law acted like a guardian, caring for and guiding people until Christ came. Now, through faith, all are children of God. Christians understand the exact role of baptism here in different ways, but all agree that it speaks of being united with Christ.

Today you can remember that your worth does not depend on your background, your achievements, or your position. If you belong to Christ, treat other believers as equals, and live each day as someone who wears the character of Jesus.
exp.3:4:
He says that Jesus came to "redeem," that is, to buy back the freedom of those who lived under the law, just as a slave was set free by paying the price for him. The purpose was that we might receive our adoption as sons: to be welcomed into God's family with all the rights of a son.
