The apostle Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, which were being pressured to depend again on the law in order to feel accepted by God. He reminds them that they used to be like children under guardians, but God sent his Son, born of a woman and subject to the law, to free them from that slavery and make them sons.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through effort or fear. If you trust in Christ, you already are a son or daughter. Today, pray to God as to a Father who receives you with affection.
exp.1:1:
Paul says that he went up to Jerusalem because of a revelation, meaning God made it known to him and led him to go. There he set before them the gospel he preaches among the Gentiles, the non-Jewish peoples. He did this privately with those recognized as leaders, the people who held the greatest standing. His concern was that he might not be running, or have already run, in vain, meaning that his work could be wasted.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were confused by people claiming that non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised. He defends that his message did not come from men, and that the leaders in Jerusalem added nothing to it. Some understand that he was not doubting his message, but wanted to show unity. Others see a real concern for the fruit of his labor.

Today, being humble does not mean keeping silent about what we believe. We can share our convictions with mature brothers and sisters, listen, and seek unity, without changing the truth of grace in Christ.
exp.5:6:
Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a person sows, they will reap in return. To reap means to gather the harvest, and God is not to be mocked means that no one can avoid the results of their actions by pretending they do not matter.

Paul writes to the believers in Galatia. Just before this, he speaks of helping one another and of sharing with those who teach the Word. With this warning, he reminds them that their choices and their generosity have consequences. What follows shows two paths: sowing for the flesh, which leads to corruption, or sowing for the Spirit, which leads to eternal life.

For today: think about what you are sowing with your time, your money, and your words. Today you can sow something good, such as supporting someone, forgiving, or giving a moment to prayer, and trust that God will make the fruit grow in its time.
exp.3:7:
Paul says that before they knew God, the Galatians served "gods" that in reality are not gods. The idea of "serving" means they lived under their control, like slaves. "By nature" means those beings had no true divine nature; they were idols or false gods.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, mostly believers of non-Jewish origin. He reminds them of their past in paganism to show the contrast: they are now children of God. He is concerned that, under the influence of other teachers, they are returning to a life bound by rules and calendars, as if they needed that to please God.

For today: ask yourself what things you seek to feel secure or valued, such as success, the approval of others, or money. Remember that in Christ you are already a beloved child of God, and you do not have to serve anything that enslaves you.
exp.0:5:
Paul says he is amazed, and troubled, that the Galatians are turning away so quickly from God, who called them by the grace of Christ, to follow a different gospel.

"Deserting" means that they are switching sides, like someone who abandons a post. "Grace" is God's favor, which cannot be earned.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Unlike his usual pattern, he does not begin this letter with his customary thanksgiving, which shows his urgency. Some teachers were insisting that, in addition to believing in Christ, people had to keep certain requirements of the law in order to be accepted by God. Paul says that this is not another good news at all, but a distortion of the true one.

For today: examine what you have added to grace in your heart, such as feeling that you must earn God's love. Rest in what Christ has already done for you, and let that move you to obey him with gratitude.
exp.0:18:
In that visit to Jerusalem, Paul saw none of the other apostles except James, whom he calls "the Lord's brother." The word "except" shows that James is the only exception. "I saw" and "I went" describe what Paul did on that trip. "The Lord's brother" is understood in different ways: many believe he was a brother of Jesus through Mary, while others see him as a close relative.

Paul writes in his letter to the Galatians. Some doubted his authority and thought his message came from the apostles in Jerusalem. He makes clear that he received the gospel directly from Jesus Christ, and that his contact with the other leaders was brief and limited. That is why he adds, almost like an oath, that he is not lying.

For today: let us be honest and clear about how we have come to believe what we believe. Let us gratefully acknowledge those whom God used along our way, but let us place our faith in Christ himself, and not only in people.
exp.3:17:
It says that it is good to have a passionate interest, or "zeal," in what is good, and that this should be constant. Being "zealous" in what is good means being fervent in pursuing what serves a noble purpose. The words "you" and "your" refer to the same readers, and "zealous" means being moved and stirred toward a goal.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being influenced by teachers who courted them with self-serving motives: they wanted the Galatians to follow them. Paul reminds them that his affection for them does not depend on his being present: it is sincere and constant. At the same time, he shows his heartfelt concern as a father worried about their faith.

For today: examine why you serve or get excited about things. Ask yourself whether your enthusiasm for doing good is constant, even when no one sees you, and whether it seeks the good of others or only your own benefit.
exp.0:14:
He says God decided, by his own will, to act in Paul's life. The phrase "was pleased" in this verse conveys that it was God's good pleasure to do so. The words "set me apart" mean that God chose Paul for a purpose, and this was from before he was born. Furthermore, God called him "by His grace," meaning as a gift that Paul did not earn. The sentence continues in the next verse: God was willing to reveal His Son in him so that he would proclaim Him among the non-Jews.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some were questioning his authority and his message. That is why he tells how he used to persecute the church and was very zealous for the Jewish traditions. His change was not his own idea or a teaching of men, but the work of God.

For today: no one is beyond the reach of God's grace, whether because of their past or their mistakes. If God has called you, trust that He is still working in your life with purpose, and respond with humility and gratitude.
exp.0:8:
As Paul said before, he now says again with firmness: if anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let that person be under a curse. To be under a curse means to be cut off, set apart, and given over to God's judgment. The phrase "a gospel contrary to the one you received" refers to a message that opposes the message of Christ.

Paul is writing to the churches of Galatia. Some people were troubling them and wanted to change the message of grace, probably by adding requirements for being saved. Paul repeats the warning so that no one takes it lightly, and he makes clear that his authority does not depend on pleasing people.

For today: compare what you hear, even when it comes from someone respected or persuasive, with what the Scriptures say about Jesus. If it adds conditions to the grace of Christ, be careful and return to the Bible.
exp.1:12:
The explanation says that the other Jewish believers in Antioch also acted hypocritically along with Peter. The word "hypocrisy" means pretending to hold one belief while actually acting on another, often out of fear. Even Barnabas, a very dear companion of Paul, was led astray by that attitude.

The speaker is Paul, who tells the Galatians what happened in Antioch. Peter had been eating with non-Jewish believers, but he pulled back when some men came from James, out of fear of what they would think. Paul confronted him because that conduct contradicted the gospel: faith in Christ unites everyone at one table.

Today, we might ask ourselves whether we change our behavior depending on who is watching us. Good examples and bad ones are contagious. Let us ask God for the courage to live with consistency and to accept correction with humility.
exp.5:4:
This verse says that each person will have to answer for their own life and their own responsibilities. The word "load" here refers to the personal weight of our actions, and "should carry" means that each one is to carry it himself.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia. A few verses earlier he asked them to help one another with heavy burdens (6:2). Now he makes clear that, even so, no one can hide behind others or compare themselves with them to feel better. Each person must examine his own work before God. Scholars note that in the original language there are two different words for "burden": one is a huge weight that needs help, and the other is personal responsibility.

Today we can help those who suffer, but without failing to carry our own load. Instead of comparing yourself with others or blaming them, ask yourself honestly: "What is mine to do today before God?"
exp.2:5:
It says that Abraham trusted God, and that God credited that trust to him as righteousness. To believe means that he relied on what God had promised him. The verse quotes Genesis 15:6, and the phrase "credited to him" means that God counted it in his favor and regarded him as being in the right. Here, righteousness means being right before God.

The apostle Paul writes to Christians in Galatia. Some were pressing them to depend on keeping the law in order to please God. Paul reminds them that they received the Spirit and saw powerful works when they heard with faith, not by keeping rules. He sets Abraham as an example: before the law, God accepted him because he believed God.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through good behavior. Trust in Him and in what Christ has done, and from there live thankfully, obeying out of love and not out of fear or to impress anyone.
exp.1:11:
He says that Peter, in Antioch, used to share meals with the believers who were not Jews. But when certain men came from James, he stopped doing so and pulled away from them. The reason was fear of "those in the circumcision group," that is, of the Jewish believers who insisted that the others keep the law of Moses. "Began to draw back and separate himself" means that he gradually pulled apart from them.

Paul is the one speaking. He writes to the churches of Galatia and recounts this episode to defend that the gospel is the same for everyone. It is not known exactly what message those men from James brought, and it has been interpreted in several ways. What is clear is that Paul saw in Peter's conduct a contradiction with the truth of the gospel.

For today: the fear of what others think can lead us to treat our brothers and sisters differently. Let us ask for courage to welcome everyone as Christ welcomed us.
exp.4:10:
Paul tells the Galatians: "Brothers, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been abolished." If he were preaching that, he says, the message of the cross would no longer be a stumbling block to people. "Offense" here means something that causes people to stumble. "Being persecuted" means enduring hardship and opposition.

Paul writes to churches in Galatia, where some teachers taught that believers had to be circumcised in order to be saved. Some think these teachers accused Paul of preaching this in other places. He answers that his suffering proves the opposite: he preached that salvation is by grace alone, through the cross, and that message offended many.

For today: the message of the cross does not depend on our merits, and at times it is uncomfortable. Let us ask for courage to proclaim it with love, without adding human requirements to make it more acceptable.
exp.4:5:
For someone joined to Christ, being Jewish (circumcised) or not Jewish (uncircumcised) makes no difference before God. What matters is faith that expresses itself through love. The word "love" here is the same word used throughout this passage, and it carries the same meaning it has elsewhere in the letter. "Expresses itself" means that faith is active and shows up in what a person does.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, to be accepted by God, they had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul answers that depending on those things means turning away from grace. True faith does not stop at a religious rule, but lives and shows itself in love.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we rely on our customs or religious achievements to feel accepted. God receives us through faith in Christ. That faith shows itself in simple things: forgiving, serving, helping, and treating others with kindness.
exp.4:1:
What it says: Paul speaks with great seriousness. "Take notice" asks you to pay close attention. When the explanation says "if you let yourselves be circumcised" and "Christ will be of no value to you at all," the point is this: if they trust in circumcision to be accepted by God, Christ no longer benefits them.

Context: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were teaching that, to be saved, non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul defends that salvation is by grace, not by adding works to Christ.

For today: Examine whether you are trusting in your efforts, rituals, or good behavior to earn God's favor. Rest in Christ, who has already done what was necessary, and obey God as a response of love, not as payment.
exp.4:19:
This verse continues the list of the "works of the flesh." It names turning to other gods or things in place of the true God (idolatry), practices of sorcery or the use of hidden powers, and attitudes that damage relationships: hatred, discord, jealousy, rage, rivalries, and divisions. The word "factions" here refers to groups that split apart out of stubbornness, rather than to false teachings in the technical sense.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being pressured to return to the law as the way of life. He reminds them that whoever is guided by the Spirit does not live under that pressure, and he shows them what life looks like without the Spirit.

Today we can ask ourselves which attitude dominates our relationships: jealousy, rage, or rivalry? Ask the Spirit to guide you, and seek to be reconciled with someone this week.
exp.4:9:
Paul says that he is confident the Galatians, joined with the Lord, will not end up holding a different view from what he taught them. He also warns that whoever is troubling or confusing them will face God's judgment, whoever that person may be. Here "troubling" means disturbing or confusing, and "take a view" means to suppose or hold the opinion that something is so.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being influenced by teachers who insisted that circumcision and the law were required for salvation. He corrects them firmly, yet he shows confidence in them. He does not name the person who was troubling them; he says "whoever he may be." This reminds us that his confidence rested in the Lord, not in the Galatians themselves.

For today: when someone confuses you with teachings that add requirements to the gospel of grace, return to Scripture and trust that God sustains his own.
exp.3:30:
It says that believers do not belong to the family of the slave woman (Hagar), but to the family of the free woman (Sarah). "Slave woman" here means a woman held in slavery, and "free" describes a woman who is not a slave. Paul concludes in this way his comparison between two sons of Abraham.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were teaching that the law of Moses had to be kept in order to be accepted by God. He uses the story of Hagar and Sarah as an illustration: Ishmael was born through human effort, and Isaac through God's promise. Paul teaches that believers are children of the promise, not of the law as a way of salvation.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through your efforts or your performance. Rest in the fact that you are his child through faith in Christ, and live with gratitude and freedom.
exp.1:10:
When Cephas came to Antioch, Paul tells us, he opposed him to his face, because Cephas stood condemned. "However" marks a contrast with what came before. "Opposed him to his face" means that he confronted him directly, and "stood condemned" means that he was in the wrong and deserved to be rebuked.

Paul writes to the Galatians to defend that the gospel is by grace, without adding the works of the law. He has just said that the leaders in Jerusalem accepted his mission. Now he shows that even Peter, so respected, was not exempt from correction. According to the following verses, Peter stopped eating with Gentile believers out of fear of the Jews, and others followed him.

For today: if we see that someone, even a beloved leader, acts against the gospel, we should speak to him with courage and respect, face to face and not behind his back. And we should also be willing to receive correction with humility.
exp.0:7:
If anyone, even Paul and his companions or an angel from heaven, were to preach a gospel that contradicts the one the Galatians had already received, that person would be "under a curse." This phrase means cursed, set apart, and handed over to God's judgment. The verse uses "preach" for what the messenger does, and "preached to you" for the message the Galatians had already heard, so the same message is in view throughout.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He is surprised that they are turning away so quickly from the grace of Christ, since some were troubling them and wanted to distort the message. Paul includes himself to show that authority does not rest in the person but in the gospel that was received. His words are very strong, but his concern is that the truth of salvation by grace not be lost.

Today, before accepting any teaching, however attractive or respected the person who gives it may be, compare it with what Christ and the apostles taught in the Bible. Follow the truth, not popularity.
exp.0:15:
He says that God was pleased to reveal his Son "in me," meaning within Paul, so that he would proclaim Jesus among the Gentiles. Right after that, Paul did not rush to consult with flesh and blood, meaning the ordinary people around him in daily life. The phrase "was pleased" means "was glad," and "consult" means "seek advice from."

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some were questioning his authority as an apostle and saying that his message came from men. That is why he tells his own story: Jesus himself called him, and he did not need others to give him permission or to teach him the gospel. The details of his travels appear in the verses that follow.

For today: When you sense that God is calling you to something, pray and seek his guidance in the Bible. Also ask for advice from wise believers, but remember that your security comes from Christ and not from the approval of people.
exp.1:13:
Paul tells how he saw that Peter and others were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel. So he spoke to Cephas in front of everyone: if you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews? The word "compel" means to force or pressure; to live like Jews means to follow the customs of the law.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Peter used to eat with believers who were not Jews, but he pulled away from them out of fear when some men sent by James arrived. His example drew others along, even Barnabas. Paul corrected him because what was at stake was that salvation comes through faith in Christ.

Today: when, out of fear of what others think, we act differently from what we believe, we need to return to the gospel. Let us be consistent and welcome as equals all who trust in Christ.
exp.3:12:
Paul reminds the Galatians that they know it was because of an illness that he first preached the gospel to them. He was sick or physically weak at that time, and they received him anyway.

Paul writes with a warm, close tone to Christians who were drifting toward the law. He recalls the affection with which they welcomed him at the beginning. We do not know with certainty what his illness was; some think of a problem with the eyes, based on verse 15, but that is only a possibility. He appeals to that relationship so that they will reflect.

For today: God can use our weakness to bless others. Do not wait until you are strong or perfect to share your faith; your sincere frailty can also show the grace of God.
exp.1:3:
It says there were "false brothers," people who were not truly believers even though they claimed to be. They came in "under false pretenses," pretending to be part of the church, in order to "spy on" the freedom we have in Christ Jesus. Their aim was "to enslave us," that is, to put us under religious rules that God did not require.

Paul is speaking, writing to the Galatians. He has just told how in Jerusalem Titus, who was a Greek, was not forced to be circumcised. Paul explains that some wanted to make circumcision a requirement for being saved. Many understand this to refer to certain Judaizers, but the text gives no further details. Paul did not give in, in order to protect the truth of the gospel.

Today, let us not allow anyone to load us with requirements that God did not ask for in order to be accepted by Him. Let us examine what we hear with the Bible in hand, and defend with humility the freedom that Christ gave us.
exp.4:25:
It says we should not become conceited, seeking the applause and recognition that are worth nothing. When we chase it, we end up provoking and challenging others, and envying one another, feeling resentment at what others have or achieve. The word here describes a disordered desire to be admired.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the churches of Galatia. He has just explained that living in the Spirit is different from living according to the flesh, and that this produces fruit such as love, peace, and patience. This verse shows a concrete sign of living according to the flesh: rivalry and envy among brothers and sisters. Paul calls them to walk in a different way.

Today, when you see that someone receives a compliment or an achievement that you wanted, pray for that person and thank God for them. In this way envy loses its strength and love grows.
exp.4:11:
Paul says he wishes that those who are unsettling the Galatians would go all the way and emasculate themselves. To unsettle means to disturb and confuse. The Berean Standard Bible's wording is strong, and the verse is commonly read as a sharp, graphic jab at those who insisted on circumcision, though scholars continue to discuss exactly how far Paul meant the words to go.

Paul writes in anger to churches confused by teachers who demanded circumcision for salvation. With very strong irony, he says that if they are so set on cutting the flesh, they should go all the way. For him, this denied the cross, where Christ had already done everything.

Today, we should not use this tone as a model for treating others. But we can learn to firmly defend the gospel of grace when someone adds requirements to what Christ has already done, and to do so with love.
exp.1:18:
It says that Paul, through the law, died to the law, so that he might live for God. The idea is that the law itself brought him to a point where he could no longer live under its rule to be accepted by God, and so he was free to live for Him.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being pressured to add the works of the law to faith in Christ. Earlier, in Galatians 2, he has argued that we are justified by Christ. Here he explains his personal experience, and the next verse clarifies it: he is crucified with Christ. Interpreters explain in various ways how the law put him to death, but all agree that he no longer depends on it to be righteous.

For today: do not spend your life trying to earn God's love by your performance. Rest in what Christ has done, and obey Him with gratitude.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that a person is not accepted by God by keeping the rules of the law of Moses, but by putting faith in Jesus Christ. "Justified" means declared righteous, forgiven, and accepted by God. "No one" means no human being. Paul says that he and the other Jewish believers also put their faith in Christ for this very reason.

The apostle Paul is speaking. He has just told how he confronted Peter in front of everyone, because Peter was pulling away from the non-Jewish believers and so implied that they needed to follow Jewish customs to be fully accepted. Paul argues that the good news is for everyone, received through faith. Paul's wording here speaks of faith in Christ, which points to Jesus as the basis of our salvation.

Today we can rest from the pressure of earning God's love. We can obey him out of gratitude, not fear, because he has already accepted us through Christ.
exp.2:2:
Paul asks a sharp question: "Are you so foolish?" He means: are they really so lacking in understanding? He reminds them that their Christian life began through the Spirit, that is, through God's work in them. So why do they now think they are finishing by the flesh, that is, by human effort and by keeping rules?

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some were teaching them that, in addition to believing in Christ, they had to keep the law of Moses. Paul, like a worried father, reminds them that they received the Spirit by hearing with faith, not by works.

Today we can fall into the same thing: believing that God accepted us by grace, yet living as if it now depends on our performance. Every day, trust God and ask him for his Spirit to grow.
exp.0:22:
They did not know Paul personally. They had only heard a report: the man who once persecuted them was now proclaiming the same faith he had tried to destroy. The phrase "preaching the faith" means that he announces the gospel, that is, what Christians believe about Jesus.

Paul is writing in his letter to the Galatians. He insists that he received the gospel from God and not from the apostles. For this reason he explains how, after his conversion, he spent time in Syria and Cilicia, far from Judea. The churches in Judea only learned of his change through what others told them, and the next verse says that because of this they glorified God.

For today: never give up on a person, and never give up on yourself. God can transform lives in a real and visible way. And when you see a change in someone, instead of holding on to distrust, you can thank God, as those churches did.
exp.2:3:
Paul asks: "Have you experienced so much for nothing?" The word "suffered" can refer to persecution or to everything they went through. Paul then adds: "if it really was for nothing," leaving a door of hope open.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, to be complete, they had to add the works of the law to their faith in Christ. Paul, concerned and firm, reminds them that they received the Spirit by believing, not by keeping rules.

For today: do not think you grow with God only through effort and rules. You began by trusting in the grace of Christ; keep walking in that same path, and let the Spirit sustain you each day.
exp.3:15:
Paul asks a question with a note of pain: "Have I now become your enemy by telling you the truth?" The word "become" in this question means that his relationship with them has changed. Paul does not accuse them in anger; he is puzzled that the relationship has changed so much.

Paul is writing to the believers in Galatia. At first they had received him with great affection, as if he were an angel. Now some teachers were influencing them to depend again on the law to be accepted by God. Paul had spoken to them clearly about the gospel of grace, and that clarity seemed to have cooled their affection.

For today: let us not confuse someone who tells us a hard truth with an enemy. Before we reject a correction, let us humbly examine whether it is true and whether it comes with love. And when it falls to us to speak, let us do it with honesty and kindness.
exp.3:14:
Here Paul asks: "What has become of the joy you once had?" Before, they felt happy because of the gospel. The word "blessing" in the verse refers to deep happiness or joy. Paul says that, if it were possible, they would have torn out their own eyes and given them to him. It was a way of saying that they loved him very much.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being influenced by teachers who were adding rules to the gospel. He reminds them of the affection they had for him when he arrived sick or weak. Some think the mention of eyes suggests a problem with eyesight, but the text does not confirm this.

For today: let us not allow our first love for Christ to grow cold. If someone tells us the truth with love, let us not see them as an enemy; rather, let us thank them for their honesty and return to the simple joy of the gospel.
exp.3:2:
This verse says that, before Christ, we were like children who lived as slaves. "Basic principles" means the elementary teachings, like the alphabet of the spiritual life. "Under the basic principles of the world" can refer to human rules, to the law seen as an early stage, or to spiritual powers; scholars interpret it in several ways.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians of Galatia. Some were wanting to return to depending on the law of Moses to be accepted by God. Paul uses the picture of an heir who is still a minor, who does not yet enjoy his inheritance because he is under guardians. In this way he explains that this stage has already passed with the coming of Christ.

For today: do not live your faith as a list of rules to earn God's favor. In Christ you are a son or daughter, not a slave. Obey out of trust and love, not out of fear.
exp.3:22:
This verse says that Abraham had two sons by two different women. The son of the slave woman, Hagar, was born according to the flesh, that is, through human effort and human planning. The son of the free woman, Sarah, was born through the promise, that is, because God had promised it and fulfilled it.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Galatia, who were being pressured to go back to depending on the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He uses the story of Abraham, Hagar, and Sarah as an illustration (he himself calls it an "allegory") to show the difference between trusting in one's own effort and trusting in God's promise.

For today: let us not try to earn God's favor through our achievements or through checklists of duties. Let us rest in what Christ has already done and in what God has promised, and live with gratitude rather than fear.
exp.2:12:
He says that Christ "redeemed" us, meaning he rescued us by paying a price, from "the curse of the law." That curse was the condemnation the law pronounced on those who did not keep it perfectly. Christ took it upon himself by becoming a curse for us. Paul quotes Deuteronomy 21:23, which said that whoever is hung on a tree is under a curse. A "tree" here means a cross or a wooden beam.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were teaching that people had to keep the law to be accepted by God. He answers that no one is made righteous by the law, but that the righteous live by faith. Christ bore the condemnation so that the blessing promised to Abraham would also reach the non-Jews.

Today, if guilt weighs on you or you feel you never measure up, remember that Christ has already borne that condemnation. Trust in what he did, and live thankful, not in fear.
exp.1:6:
They said that the leaders in Jerusalem recognized that God had entrusted Paul with preaching the gospel to those who were not Jews (the "uncircumcised"), just as he had entrusted Peter with preaching it to the Jews (the "circumcised").

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia to defend that the gospel comes by grace, without adding the law of Moses to it. Here he tells how Peter, James, and John did not impose anything more on him, but recognized his calling. In this way he shows that his message was the same as theirs.

For today: God calls different people to serve in different ways. Instead of comparing ourselves or competing, we can recognize and support the work of other believers, while all of us stand firm in the same gospel of Christ.
exp.3:9:
Paul says that the Galatians are carefully observing special days, months, seasons, and years. He is referring to religious celebrations and calendars that they had started to keep as though they were necessary.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, worried that some were trying to bring them under Jewish law. It is not certain whether he means only Jewish festivals or also pagan customs; scholars understand it in several ways. What is clear is that Paul fears his work among them may have been in vain, and he addresses them affectionately as brothers.

For today: examine whether any religious habit has become a burden or a way of trying to earn God's favor. Days and practices can help us worship, but our relationship with God rests on his grace, not on keeping a calendar.
exp.3:11:
Paul makes a tender appeal: "Brothers, I beg you, become like me, for I became like you." He adds that they have done him no wrong, meaning they have caused him no offense or personal harm.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were turning back toward religious practices such as keeping days, months, and years, as if doing so would bring them salvation. Paul, a Jew, had stopped depending on the law to be made right before God, and he identified himself with them, who were not Jews. He reminds them that there is no resentment between them, and he appeals to the good relationship they once shared. Some think he means that they should live free from the law as he does; the text does not clarify this further.

For today: when we need to correct someone, let us do it with gentleness, remembering the relationship and free of resentment, seeking their good and not winning an argument.
exp.2:16:
Paul says that God made a covenant with Abraham, and that this covenant was established beforehand with a view to Christ. The law came 430 years later, and it does not revoke that covenant or nullify the promise. Here "covenant" means the agreement God made, and "revoke" means to cancel or make something no longer valid.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being influenced to believe that they had to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. To answer them, he uses the example of a human agreement, which no one changes once it has been established. The 430 years is a figure Paul takes from the biblical tradition (Exodus 12:40), and some scholars discuss how it is calculated.

For today: you do not need to earn God's love through your own effort. His promise in Christ is firm. Rest in his faithfulness and obey him out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.3:16:
They show a lot of interest in the Galatians, but their motives are wrong. The phrase "they are zealous for you" means they eagerly seek them out. "Isolate you from us" means they want to cut them off and leave them on the outside. Their goal is that the Galatians will then become eager for them and look up to them.

The apostle Paul is writing to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were pushing them to add the law as a requirement for being saved. Paul fears they will lose the freedom of the gospel. Scholars disagree about exactly who these teachers were, but the context points to those teachers.

For today: do not confuse attention with true love. Ask yourself whether the person who encourages you to follow them brings you closer to Christ or only to their own influence. A good guide leads you to Jesus, not to depending on them.
exp.4:23:
This verse says that those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. The "flesh" is our human nature inclined toward what is wrong. The "passions" are the emotions that pull us out of line, and the "desires" are the strong urges to do what God does not approve. To crucify is to put them to death, to reject them as someone who no longer gives them command.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He has just contrasted the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit. He wants them to understand that belonging to Christ changes the way one lives. Then he encourages them to walk in the Spirit and not fall into vain conceit or envy.

For today: when a desire arises that pulls you away from God, such as anger, envy, or pride, do not feed it. Pray and decide to obey the Spirit in that moment, trusting that Christ gives you strength.
exp.3:6:
This verse says that the believer no longer lives as a slave, but as a child of God. And since he is a child, he also receives an inheritance from God, and receives it through Christ. "Slave" here means someone who belongs to a master, and "heir" is the one who receives what the Father has prepared for his children.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, who is writing to the churches of Galatia. Some were beginning to depend again on the law to feel accepted by God. Paul reminds them that Christ redeemed them, that God adopted them, and that the Spirit gives them the confidence to cry out to God in a close and familiar way.

For today: when you feel guilty or think you must earn God's love, remember who you are. You do not pray like a slave who fears, but like a beloved child. Come near to God with confidence, and obey him out of love, not out of fear.
exp.3:3:
When the appointed time had fully come, God sent his Son. Jesus was born of a woman, which means he was truly human, and he lived under the law of Moses. "Under the law" means that he was under its authority. "The time had fully come" refers to the set time, arrived at its full measure.

The apostle Paul writes to the Galatians, who were turning back to depend on the law to be accepted by God. Earlier he compared a child heir, who lives under guardians until the date his father has set. Paul shows that the coming of Christ marks the move from that stage to the freedom of the children of God.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through religious effort. Christ came for you, so you can approach God with confidence, as a child to his father. And when life seems slow or confusing, remember that God knows when to act.
exp.2:7:
The Scripture foresaw that God would declare non-Jewish people right with him by faith, so God announced the good news to Abraham in advance, promising him: "All nations will be blessed through you." The word "foretold" means that it spoke ahead of time about the good news, and "justify" means to declare someone righteous.

Paul writes to the Galatians, believers who were being pressured to add the works of the law of Moses to their faith in Christ. To answer them, Paul reminds them of Abraham, who was accepted by God because he believed, long before the law existed. In this way he shows that God's plan has always included all peoples.

For today: no one has to earn God's favor through effort or merit. Trust God as Abraham did, and welcome others with joy, regardless of their background, because the promise is for everyone.
exp.0:13:
Paul says that in Judaism he was advancing ahead of many of his contemporaries, people his own age and from his own nation. The word "advancing" in the verse means making progress or moving forward. "Zealous" means very eager and passionate. The "traditions of my fathers" were the religious teachings and customs handed down by his ancestors.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were questioning his authority and teaching a different gospel. For that reason he recalls his past: he did not receive the message from other men, but from Jesus Christ. If anyone had reason to follow only tradition, it was he, yet God transformed him.

For today: we can have great religious zeal and still be mistaken. Let us examine our customs and efforts in the light of Christ, and ask God for humility to follow Him, not only what we have always done.
exp.2:27:
It says that, for God, the differences that divide people are not what decides who belongs to his family. Where the text says "slave," that means someone who is owned by another person; "free" means a free person; and "male" means a man, while "female" means a woman. "You are all one" means that all of you are one. Believers form one family in Christ.

Paul writes to the churches in Galatia, where some were teaching that non-Jewish believers had to follow the law of Moses in order to be accepted. Paul answers that faith in Christ, not one's background or the law, makes us children of God and heirs of the promise made to Abraham. The verses before this one speak of baptism as being "clothed with Christ."

For today: in the church and in everyday life, treat each person as a brother or sister in Christ, regardless of nationality, social class, or gender. This week, look for ways to reach out to someone who is different from you.
exp.1:19:
He says that Paul sees himself as united with Christ in his death: his old way of living, centered on himself, was crucified. Now Christ lives in him. The phrase "with Christ" reflects the sense of being joined to Christ, and "in the body" refers to his daily life in this physical life. Paul lives by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself up for him.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were teaching that the law of Moses had to be kept in order to be made right with God. He answers that the law does not save, and that the new life comes through faith in Christ. For that reason he adds that he does not set aside the grace of God.

Today, when facing a decision or a burden, we can ask ourselves: "Am I acting out of pride or fear, or trusting in the love of Christ?" Bringing that moment to God in prayer helps us live supported by his grace, not by our own effort.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that, since we are already children of God, he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts. That Spirit leads us to cry out, that is, to call out with confidence, "Abba, Father!" "Abba" is an Aramaic word that was used affectionately to mean "daddy" or "father."

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being tempted to return to the law as the way to please God. He reminds them that Christ came to redeem us and to give us adoption as children. Because of this, we no longer live as servants, but as children and heirs.

Today you can come near to God without fear or pretense. When you pray, speak to him like a beloved child speaking with his Father, even if you feel weak or do not know what to say. The Spirit accompanies you in that prayer.
exp.0:19:
Paul solemnly assures his readers that what he is writing is true. "I assure you before God" means he speaks as if God himself were watching him. "No lie" is plain: he is not exaggerating or making anything up.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some were questioning him and saying that his message came only from the apostles in Jerusalem. He answers that he received the gospel directly from Jesus Christ, and he tells how, after three years, he visited Peter and saw James, but no other apostles. That is why he swears that his account is true. His authority as an apostle was at stake.

For today: watch your words as if you were speaking before God, because you are. Be honest, even when no one can check what you say.
exp.5:3:
This verse says that each person should honestly examine their own work and conduct. If in doing so they find something good, they can take satisfaction in that very thing, without comparing themselves to others. "Work" means what a person does; here, "reason to boast" refers to a healthy sense of accomplishment, not to fame.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He speaks of helping one another with burdens and of not thinking themselves better than others. Just before this, he warns that whoever thinks himself to be something is deceiving himself. He then adds that each person will bear their own load. Some see here a balance between helping others and taking responsibility for oneself.

For today: before you criticize or compare yourself to someone, take a few minutes to ask God how you are doing. Give thanks for what is good, correct what needs correcting, and find your satisfaction in your own honest work rather than in how you measure up to others.
exp.3:8:
Paul tells the Galatians that they already know God. Then he corrects himself: what matters even more is that God knows them and chose them. So he asks, sadly, why they would turn back to those weak and worthless principles, which are feeble and unable to save. "Turning back" means returning to something you had left behind, and "weak" means without strength.

Paul wrote this letter to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, to please God, they had to keep the Jewish law, with its days and festivals. Paul reminds them that in Christ they are already children and heirs, not slaves. Interpreters debate exactly what these "principles" were, but all agree that they were human or religious rules that enslave.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we trust our religious practices to earn God's love. Rest in this: God already knows you and has received you as his child through Christ.
exp.0:21:
He says that Paul was not personally known to the Christian churches of Judea, the believers who were in Christ, meaning joined to Jesus through faith.

In this letter Paul argues that he received the gospel directly from Christ, not from the apostles. After his conversion, he spent years in Arabia, Damascus, Syria, and Cilicia, and he visited Jerusalem only briefly. That is why he explains that the churches of Judea did not know him in person; they had only heard of his change. Some interpreters see here that his message did not depend on the approval of those churches.

For today: a transformed life speaks for itself. Even when others do not know us closely, our change in Christ can lead people to give glory to God. Let us live with sincerity, without seeking fame.

sum.0: Paul greets the churches of Galatia and expresses his surprise that they have turned away so quickly from the gospel of Christ's grace to follow a different, distorted message. He affirms that his gospel came through a revelation from Jesus Christ, not from human beings, and he describes how God changed him from a persecutor of the church into a preacher of the faith, for the glory of God.
sum.3: Paul explains that when the right time came, God sent his Son to redeem us and make us children and heirs, not slaves. That is why he is concerned that the Galatians want to go back to depending on the law. Using the allegory of Hagar and Sarah, he teaches that we are children of the promise and of freedom.
sum.2: Paul rebukes the Galatians for wanting to be made complete by works of the law, when they received the Spirit through faith. He teaches them that Abraham was justified by faith and that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. God's promise still stands, and all who believe in Christ are children of God and heirs.
sum.5: Paul encourages believers to gently restore anyone who falls into sin, to help carry one another's burdens, and to keep doing good without growing weary, sowing for the Spirit. He warns against those who insist on circumcision in order to avoid persecution. He states that he boasts only in the cross of Christ, since what matters is becoming a new creation.
sum.4: Paul urges the Galatians to stand firm in the freedom that Christ gave them, and not to go back under the law or circumcision again, because what counts is faith working through love. He calls them to serve one another, to walk by the Spirit rather than according to the flesh, and to produce the fruit of the Spirit.
sum.1: Paul recounts that he went up to Jerusalem, where the leaders approved his message to the Gentiles and did not require Titus to be circumcised. He then confronted Peter in Antioch for pulling away from the Gentiles out of fear. He teaches that we are made right with God through faith in Christ, not through the works of the law, and that Christ lives within the believer.
